why: The statement asks whether all regular languages can be expressed with 'limited' star nesting depth. Read per language, that is trivially true. Its only substantive reading is whether one uniform bound N works for every regular language. A proven uniform bound of 3, 4 or 13 therefore answers the statement as worded, so all three OpenAI manuscripts, and the bundled openai-math-134 entry, are scored 'whole'. They are not scored 'bound': the statement asks only whether some finite bound exists, not for the least one. Whether height one always suffices is the question in the Wikipedia article's wider literature, but the statement does not ask it. None of these events has expert review, and the Lean file leaves the main theorem as a sorry, so all are unreviewed. I scored them doubtful rather than credible because of the landmark claim with no uptake yet, the inconsistent descriptions of the thirteen-bound method, and the release's other withdrawals. Only about a week has passed, and no specific error has been identified, so not_credible would be too strong. The AI role is 'generated' on each OpenAI event. The author line is 'OpenAI' alone, the README credits the internal model with the release's results, and this family is not among the listed exceptions. Among the pre-snapshot events, Pin–Straubing–Thérien and Bourne–Ruškuc settle restricted classes and appeared in journals, so they are 'case' and 'digested'. The Bourne thesis is a 'case', but the record names no committee approval, so it stays unreviewed. Eggan, Hashiguchi, Kirsten and Bojańczyk concern ordinary star height, and Danieli concerns Parikh images over infinite alphabets, so all five are variants. The ProofAtlas entry states no result.
doubts: openai-math-134 duplicates the three per-paper events; it is scored identically to them, so double-counting changes nothing. The AI attribution rests on the README's release-wide statement, not on a statement about this family. A reader who takes the problem to ask whether height one suffices would score these events as a bound, or as a case, rather than whole; I followed the statement's wording. The Oct 8 commit may have changed the Lean file, and the record does not say whether it did. The dates of the pre-snapshot classic results come from secondary sources. That does not affect which side of the snapshot they fall on.
